sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Post-hoc image explanations usually show where a model looks using spatial heatmaps or indicate which channels matter using global channel scores. These separate views are limiting for multispectral data because channel relevance is often spatially localized and physically meaningful. We introduce Spectral-Spatial Interpretation (SSI), a full-grid attribution method over position-channel players (g,c). For each spatial position, SSI fixes the observed surrounding context, defines a conditional game over the channels at that position, and applies the Shapley value to this local game. The result is a full spectral-spatial attribution matrix rather than a single heatmap or a global channel ranking. SSI has a clear local interpretation. It satisfies Shapley fairness within each position, and aggregating its channel attributions exactly recovers the position-level contextual contrast obtained by replacing that position with the baseline. SSI also differs from context-averaged Owen-style hierarchical accounting, which uses the same position-channel grouping but averages over external spatial coalitions. On HLS Burn Scar, SSI outperforms an MC-Owen estimator across retained attribution metrics while using only about 6% of its evaluation budget. Across CUB-200, EuroSAT, and HLS Burn Scar under both per-channel mean and zero baselines, SSI achieves the best joint deletion and insertion AUC over dense, flat, and rank-1 baselines, yields the strongest spectral hit rates and channel deletion, and leads spatial localization on both annotated datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/AtheavenMa/Spectral-Spatial-Interpretation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Modern vision models increasingly operate on inputs with multiple physically meaningful channels, from RGB fine-grained recognition to Sentinel-2 land-cover classification and burn-scar mapping. Existing post-hoc explanations usually answer where the model looks, but not which spectral channels support the prediction at each location. For these data, high attribution to near-infrared at vegetation boundary or to short-wave infrared within burn scar reflects different physical evidence from attribution to visible bands. An explanation should therefore identify where the evidence lies, which channels support it, and how much each channel contributes at each location. Existing methods collapse this structure in one of two ways. Spatial attribution methods such as GradCAM [Selvaraju et al., 2017], RISE [Petsiuk et al., 2018], and Extremal Perturbation [Fong et al., 2019] aggregate over channels and produce single heatmap. Spectral or channel attribution methods rank bands globally using mutual information, attention weights, or SHAP-style scores [Lundberg and Lee, 2017], averaging channel effects across space. Even two-stage pipeline that multiplies spatial heatmap by global channel vector assumes rank-1 structure, A(g, c) = s(g)q(c), meaning that the same channel profile applies everywhere. This assumption fails when different regions have different spectral signatures, as with red and blue plumage on bird or vegetation and water in Preprint. Figure 1: Spectral channels carry spatially distinct physical information. On Painted Bunting (a), the red belly, green back, and blue head each align with different RGB channel; on Sentinel-2 scene (b), water, forest, and built-up areas align with B3, B8A, and B12. SSI is designed to recover this joint spectral-spatial structure. satellite scene (Figure 1). Channel importance depends on location. The same band can be decisive in one region and irrelevant in another, so the attribution target should be localized position-channel score rather than global channel ranking. Φ(g, c) identifying where evidence lies and spectral scores (cid:80) We introduce Spectral-Spatial Interpretation (SSI), full-grid attribution method that assigns score Φ(g, c) to each grid cell and channel (Figure 2). For each position, SSI fixes the rest of the image to its observed values and applies the standard Shapley value only to the channels at that position. The contribution lies in the observed-context position game rather than new allocation rule. The output can be used directly as joint attribution matrix or aggregated into spatial scores (cid:80) Φ(g, c) identifying which channels contribute, without assuming rank-1 spatial-spectral factorization. This observed-context formulation gives SSI local Shapley fairness and contextual aggregation consistency. In particular, (cid:80) Φ(g, c) equals the full-context contrast of replacing the entire position with the baseline. Unlike context-averaged Owen-style hierarchical attribution [Owen, 1977], which averages over external spatial coalitions, SSI targets localized spectral evidence and solves small channel-player games at each position. We evaluate SSI on CUB-200 [Wah et al., 2011], EuroSAT [Helber et al., 2019], and HLS Burn Scar [Phillips et al., 2023]. Across all three datasets, SSI outperforms dense, flat, and rank-1 attribution baselines on joint position-channel faithfulness metrics, and on HLS Burn Scar it further outperforms an MC-Owen estimator while using only about 6% of its evaluation budget. Our contributions are as follows: We formulate spectral-spatial interpretation as attribution over position-channel players (g, c), targeting localized channel evidence rather than only heatmap or global channel ranking. We define SSI as an observed-context attribution method that fixes the surrounding image context and applies standard Shapley allocation among channels at each position. We characterize its local Shapley fairness, contextual aggregation consistency, and distinction from context-averaged Owen-style accounting. Across CUB-200, EuroSAT, and HLS Burn Scar under both per-channel mean and zero baselines, SSI achieves the best joint deletion, rank-1 deletion, and grid-sum insertion AUC over dense, flat, and rank-1 baselines. It leads spectral hit rates and channel deletion on EuroSAT and HLS Burn Scar, as well as spatial localization on both annotated datasets. On HLS Burn Scar, SSI also outperforms MC-Owen using about 6% of its evaluation budget. 2 Figure 2: Overview of SSI. For each spatial position g, SSI fixes the observed surrounding context and allocates the local contribution among channels, producing full joint attribution matrix Φ(g, c) for spatial and spectral interpretation.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Post-hoc spatial attribution. large family of explanation methods produces spatial heatmaps indicating which image regions drive prediction. Gradient-based approaches such as Integrated Gradients [Sundararajan et al., 2017] and Grad-CAM [Selvaraju et al., 2017] propagate target-class signals to pixels or activation maps. Perturbation-based approaches such as RISE [Petsiuk et al., 2018] and Extremal Perturbation [Fong et al., 2019] measure prediction changes under spatial masks. These methods are effective for identifying where evidence lies, but their explanations either aggregate over channels or treat input elements independently. They therefore do not provide principled decomposition of which spectral channels matter at each location. Spectral and channel attribution. complementary line of work ranks spectral bands or channels using mutual information [Feng et al., 2014], game-theoretic criteria [Bruce, 2013], attention weights [Hu et al., 2018, Woo et al., 2018], or SHAP-style attribution [Lundberg and Lee, 2017]. Such methods are useful for identifying globally important wavelengths, but they typically average channel relevance over space. This averaging can hide localized spectral evidence because band may be unimportant on average yet decisive in small region. SSI instead assigns attribution to each position-channel pair and preserves spatial variation in channel importance. Joint spectral-spatial modeling. Architectures such as 3D CNNs [Chen et al., 2016], spectralspatial transformers [Dang et al., 2022], and factorized architecture search [Zhong et al., 2022] jointly exploit spectral and spatial information but focus on prediction performance, and their internal representations remain opaque. Propagation-based explanations have been adapted for hyperspectral classifiers [Nagasubramanian et al., 2018], but remain architecture-specific. SSI instead provides model-agnostic, game-theoretic attribution for already-trained models. Game-theoretic and hierarchical attribution. Shapley values [Shapley, 1953] and SHAP-style methods [Lundberg and Lee, 2017] provide additive feature attributions but usually treat all interpretable units as flat players. This flat treatment does not reflect the natural position-channel hierarchy of multispectral images. The Shapley interaction index [Grabisch and Roubens, 1999] and its higher-order extensions [Sundararajan et al., 2020, Tsai et al., 2023] quantify synergies but do not exploit this two-level structure. Group-level Shapley methods [Jullum et al., 2021] treat each predefined group as an atomic player and do not decompose contributions within groups; methods addressing feature dependence [Aas et al., 2022] estimate conditional expectations rather than fixing observed context. SSI differs from both lines of work in its attribution units and treatment of context. Owen value. The Owen value [Owen, 1977], building on games with coalition structures [Aumann and Drèze, 1974], respects priori coalitions by allocating value across and within groups. SSI uses the same position-channel grouping but targets observed-context conditional attribution rather than context-averaged hierarchical accounting.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate the faithfulness of SSIs joint position-channel attribution Φ(g, c) using deletion and insertion AUC. We then examine how rank-1 spatial-spectral factorization affects this attribution and assess spatial and spectral aggregation through localization, channel deletion, and spectral hit rates. Qualitative case studies are presented in 4.4, with full metric curves in the appendix. We also compare SSI with stronger gradient-based baselines on HLS Burn Scar and evaluate faithfulness using ROAD. 4.1 Experimental Setup Datasets and models. We evaluate SSI on three datasets covering RGB images, multispectral land-cover classification, and burn-scar mapping. CUB-200-2011 [Wah et al., 2011] contains RGB images of 200 bird species with bounding-box annotations. We fine-tune an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 classifier. EuroSAT [Helber et al., 2019] contains 13-band Sentinel-2 patches from 10 land-use/land-cover classes. We train ResNet-18 classifier from scratch on all bands. HLS Burn Scar [Phillips et al., 2023] contains 6-band Harmonized LandsatSentinel-2 patches with burn-scar masks. We train lightweight UNet for burn-scar segmentation and use the burn-class logit averaged over ground-truth mask positions as the scalar response for attribution. Training details and model performance are reported in Appendix B. Player space and baselines. All methods are evaluated on the same full position-channel player space (g, c). To balance spatial resolution and computational cost, we use an 8 8 grid on EuroSAT and HLS Burn Scar and finer 16 16 grid on CUB-200 to capture more detailed spatial structure. We use per-channel mean baseline as the primary masking value in all datasets and methods; to verify robustness to baseline choice, we also report results with zero baseline. The semantics of the conditional game wg depend on this choice, as is inherent to all perturbation-based attribution. We compare SSI against three classes of attribution methods. The dense and flat baselines include Integrated Gradients (IG) [Sundararajan et al., 2017], DeepSHAP [Lundberg and Lee, 2017, Shrikumar et al., 2017], and KernelSHAP [Lundberg and Lee, 2017]. Dense maps from IG and DeepSHAP are summed within each position-channel player; KernelSHAP directly treats each (g, c) as an interpretable feature. We also include rank-1 perturbation control based on RISE [Petsiuk et al., 2018]. This method forms factorized attribution map A(g, c) = s(g)q(c), where s(g) is spatial importance score and q(c) is global channel score obtained from the target-logit drop caused by masking channel globally across all spatial positions. It tests whether spatial heatmap multiplied by global channel vector is sufficient for joint spectral-spatial explanation. Finally, SSI computes the full-context attribution Φ(g, c) for every grid cell and channel. On HLS Burn Scar, we also compare against Expected Gradients [Erion et al., 2021], Guided IG [Kapishnikov et al., 2021], and FullGrad [Srinivas and Fleuret, 2019]; these additional comparisons are reported separately in 4.6. Methods with dense channel-resolved attribution maps are aggregated spatially within grid cells while retaining the channel dimension for joint evaluation; channel summation is performed only for 6 spatial summaries. Baseline descriptions are in Appendix B.2, and evaluation budgets for the original methods are reported in Appendix B.3. Metrics. All evaluations use the target-class logit, matching the value function in 3.1. Lower deletion AUC indicates better attribution, whereas higher insertion AUC, bbox mIoU, and spectral hit rates indicate better results. Joint deletion operates directly on ranked position-channel players. Rank-1 projection evaluates each method under the best rank-1 factorization of its attribution matrix into spatial heatmap and global channel profile. For insertion, we sum attribution scores over channels at each grid position and insert positions in decreasing order of the aggregated score, which evaluates the spatial summary and ensures comparability with rank-1 baselines like RISE. A(g, c), while spectral aggregation uses Ach(c) = (cid:80) A(g, c). For spectral hit rates, we compare the top-ranked channels against dataset-specific physical priors grounded in established spectral indices (e.g., Normalized Burn Ratio for burn scars, NDVI/NDRE for vegetation). Only bands with well-documented physical correlations are included; classes without reliably positive spectral signature are excluded. The full prior specification and scientific justification are given in Appendix C.3. 4.2 Joint Faithfulness SSI assigns attribution to full-grid position-channel players (g, c). We therefore evaluate faithfulness by ranking the same players and measuring how efficiently the ranking removes target-class evidence. Our primary metric is joint deletion AUC: players are masked in decreasing attribution order, and the target-class logit is recorded after each step. Lower AUC indicates that the attribution ranking removes full-context evidence earlier. We also report rank-1 deletion diagnostic. For each method, we reshape the attribution scores into matrix RCN , where is the number of spatial cells, and retain only its leading rank-1 approximation. This factorized map has the form A(g, c) a(g)b(c), corresponding to spatial heatmap multiplied by global channel profile. If such factorization were sufficient, rank-1 deletion would preserve joint faithfulness. Table 1 shows that SSI achieves the lowest joint deletion AUC and the highest insertion AUC on all three datasets under both the per-channel mean and zero baselines. On CUB-200 under the mean baseline, SSI improves joint deletion over IG and DeepSHAP and achieves the highest insertion AUC (.7132), surpassing RISE (.6886) despite RISE using 8,000 spatial masks versus 2048 for SSI. The differences are larger on EuroSAT and HLS Burn Scar, where SSI removes target evidence substantially earlier than all baselines under both deletion metrics. These results support the use of Φ(g, c) as full-context position-channel attribution score and suggest that the advantage is not driven by particular baseline choice. SSI also performs consistently across the tested grid resolutions, as shown in Appendix C.4. We also evaluate faithfulness using ROAD [Rong et al., 2022] on HLS Burn Scar. SSI achieves the highest LeRF AUC (.657) and lowest MoRF AUC (.1143) among nine evaluated methods under this complementary removal protocol. Appendix C.2 reports the full comparison. The rank-1 diagnostic further shows that factorized spectral-spatial explanations are insufficient. RISE can provide strong spatial or global-channel signals, but its rank-1 deletion AUC remains substantially worse than SSI. The gap between joint and rank-1 deletion is smallest on CUB-200 (C=3) and largest on EuroSAT (C=13), suggesting that the rank-1 approximation degrades as channel diversity increases. Thus, spatial heatmap multiplied by global channel vector cannot replace the full joint attribution matrix. 4.3 Spatial and Spectral Aggregation We assess whether the full position-channel attribution matrix remains meaningful after aggregation. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced Spectral-Spatial Interpretation (SSI), which explains predictions of multi-channel image models at the level of joint position-channel players (g, c). SSI fixes the observed surrounding context and allocates each positions contribution among its channels via the Shapley value, producing full attribution matrix whose channel aggregation exactly recovers the position-level contextual contrast. Across CUB-200, EuroSAT, and HLS Burn Scar, SSI improves joint faithfulness, spectral hit rates, and channel deletion over dense, flat, and rank-1 baselines, and outperforms MC-Owen on HLS Burn Scar with roughly 6% of its evaluation budget. ln and its per-image cost grows only linearly in Although SSIs estimation error grows only as (Appendix B.4), applying SSI to hyperspectral sensors with hundreds of correlated bands may benefit from channel screening or adaptive grouping to reduce spectral redundancy before local Shapley allocation. Validating such extensions on operational hyperspectral missions remains future work. SSI may also be useful for imaging spectroscopy data from sensors such as EnMAP, where spectral channels carry spatially localized physical information. The observed-context formulation may extend to other multi-channel imaging domains with localized physical meaning, including biomedical microscopy and industrial materials inspection. Code availability. The open-source SSI implementation and its usage documentation are available at https://github.com/AtheavenMa/Spectral-Spatial-Interpretation.

sections.title: B Additional Experimental Details
sections.content: B.1 Datasets, Models, and Preprocessing CUB-200-2011. CUB-200-2011 [Wah et al., 2011] contains 11,788 RGB images of 200 bird species. Each image is annotated with bounding box, part keypoints, and binary attributes, including color attributes. We fine-tune an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 classifier and use the ground-truth class logit as the scalar response for attribution. EuroSAT. EuroSAT [Helber et al., 2019] contains 27,000 Sentinel-2 patches from 10 land-use/landcover classes. We use the 13-band version, including visible RGB, red-edge, near-infrared, short-wave infrared, and atmospheric bands. We train ResNet-18 classifier from scratch on all 13 bands. HLS Burn Scar. HLS Burn Scar [Phillips et al., 2023] contains Harmonized LandsatSentinel-2 patches with six spectral bands: Blue, Green, Red, NIR, SWIR 1, and SWIR 2. We train lightweight UNet for burn-scar segmentation. For attribution and evaluation, we average the burn-class logit over the evaluation region to obtain scalar response. 18 Training and robustness. Full optimizer settings, learning rates, epochs, and preprocessing choices are dataset-specific and fixed before attribution evaluation. B.2 Attribution Baseline Details Integrated Gradients. We compute Integrated Gradients (IG) [Sundararajan et al., 2017] along straight-line path from the masking baseline to the input using 300 integration steps. IG produces dense attributions in RCHW . To match the common player space, we sum pixel-level attributions within each grid cell and channel, yielding one score for every position-channel player (g, c). DeepSHAP. DeepSHAP [Lundberg and Lee, 2017, Shrikumar et al., 2017] combines DeepLIFTstyle propagation rules with Shapley-value approximation. We compute DeepSHAP with 1,000 background samples. As with IG, dense attributions are aggregated within each grid cell and channel to obtain scores over the same (g, c) player space. KernelSHAP. For KernelSHAP [Lundberg and Lee, 2017], each position-channel pair (g, c) is treated as an interpretable feature. We use the same spatial grid as SSI and sample 2P + 2048 coalitions following the library default, where the first 2P are deterministic singleton and complement pairs that receive the highest Shapley kernel weights, and the remaining 2048 are drawn uniformly at random. KernelSHAP is therefore the flat-Shapley baseline most directly matched to SSIs player granularity, but it does not impose the position-level coalition structure used by SSI. RISE rank-1 control. We include RISE-based rank-1 control [Petsiuk et al., 2018]. RISE estimates spatial importance map srise(g) by generating =8000 random binary masks, evaluating the model response under each masked input, and computing weighted average of the masks. We combine this spatial score with global channel score q(c), defined as the target-logit drop caused by masking channel globally across all spatial positions: Arise(g, c) = srise(g) q(c). This gives strong spatial perturbation baseline, but its rank-1 structure forces channel relevance to be global rather than varying by position. Comparing SSI against this control isolates the benefit of preserving the full joint attribution matrix rather than factorizing it into spatial and spectral summaries. Additional gradient-based baselines on HLS Burn Scar. We additionally compare against Expected Gradients [Erion et al., 2021], which averages gradient-based contributions across reference samples and interpolation points; Guided IG [Kapishnikov et al., 2021], which adapts the integration path; and FullGrad [Srinivas and Fleuret, 2019], which incorporates input and internal bias-gradient information. All reported scores are evaluated over the same HLS Burn Scar position-channel players and using the metrics of Appendix C.1. For dense input-channel attributions, pixel-level scores are summed within each grid cell while retaining their channel indices. Unlike these input-channel attribution methods, FullGrad also includes internal bias-gradient terms; its conversion to positionchannel scores is implementation-specific rather than direct spatial sum of native input-channel tensor. SSI. SSI computes the full-context attribution Φ(g, c) from Eq. (6) over the full position-channel player set. No search-selected support is used for the reported main metrics. The resulting map is evaluated directly as joint attribution matrix and can also be summarized spatially by (cid:80) Φ(g, c) or spectrally by (cid:80) Φ(g, c). B.3 Computational Cost We distinguish the permutation count K, the number of channel orderings sampled in each cells conditional game wg as used in Proposition 2, from the evaluation count Neval, the total number of model forward passes needed to produce all attribution scores for one image. Reading Eq. (9) as literal recipe, each sampled permutation π requires evaluating wg on the C+1 cumulative subsets , {c1}, {c1, c2}, . . . , Sg. Since wg()=0 requires no model evaluation and the endpoint v(Bg) is shared across all permutations at the same cell, the per-cell forward-pass count is bounded by K(C+1) in the worst case and is closer to K(C1)+2 when endpoint states are cached. We report 19 the worst-case upper bound throughout to keep the comparison conservative; cached implementations only reduce SSIs cost further. For the small-C regime where SSI enumerates all subsets, the analogous bound is 2C per cell. Table 4 reports Neval for every method under this convention. SSI enumerates all channel subsets when 2C 10 (CUB-200 with C=3, giving 2C evaluations) and switches to permutation sampling with K=10 otherwise (EuroSAT with C=13 and HLS with C=6, giving up to K(C+1) evaluations). sections.content: C.1 Metric Definitions Joint deletion Joint deletion starts from the original input and masks position-channel players (g, c) in decreasing order of signed attribution score. The target-class logit is recorded after each step. Lower deletion AUC and higher insertion AUC indicate better results. 20 Rank-1 projection. For each method, we reshape the grid-level attribution scores into matrix RCN , where is the number of channels and is the number of grid cells. We compute the best rank-1 approximation (cid:98)A = σ1u1v 1 , where σ1 is the largest singular value and u1, v1 are the corresponding singular vectors. Deletion and insertion are then evaluated using (cid:98)A. Spatial aggregation. Spatial maps are obtained by summing over channels: Asp(g) = A(g, c). (cid:88) We threshold Asp at multiple top-coverage levels and compute mIoU with available spatial annotations. CUB uses bird bounding boxes, and HLS uses burn-scar masks or their spatial support. Spectral aggregation. Channel scores are obtained by summing over spatial cells: Ach(c) = A(g, c). (cid:88) Channel deletion masks entire channels in decreasing Ach(c) order. Spectral hit rates compare the top-ranked channels against dataset-specific spectral priors: Hit@K = TopK(A) Ty Ty , averaged over correctly classified samples. C.2 ROAD Faithfulness Evaluation We also evaluate SSI with Remove and Debias (ROAD) [Rong et al., 2022] on HLS Burn Scar as complementary faithfulness check to the standard masking-based deletion and insertion tests. The evaluation compares methods on the same position-channel player space, reporting ROAD area under the curve for removing the most relevant features first (MoRF; lower is better) and the least relevant features first (LeRF; higher is better). ROAD is intended to mitigate some evaluation artifacts introduced by feature removal, rather than eliminate every distribution-shift effect. Table 5 reports the results included in the author rebuttal. SSI performs best in both removal directions among the nine methods considered. Table 5: ROAD evaluation on HLS Burn Scar. C.3 Spectral Band Priors The spectral hit-rate evaluation (4.3) requires set of prior bands for each class. These are channels whose reflectance is expected to be positively associated with the target-class decision. We select these priors from established spectral indices and physical reasoning rather than the attribution results themselves. 21 HLS Burn Scar. The HLS Burn Scar dataset uses six-band stack (Blue, Green, Red, Narrow NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2) derived from the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 product [Claverie et al., 2018]. For the burn-scar class, we designate Red (band 2), SWIR1 (band 4), and SWIR2 (band 5) as prior bands. This selection follows directly from the Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR) and its variants, which are the standard spectral indices for burn severity mapping [Key and Benson, 2006, García and Caselles, 1991]. Burned surfaces exhibit elevated SWIR reflectance due to exposed soil, charcoal, and ash, and elevated red reflectance due to the loss of chlorophyll absorption [Trigg and Flasse, 2001]. These spectral signatures have been validated across decades of fire-mapping literature using Landsat TM/ETM+/OLI and Sentinel-2 MSI sensors. NIR is excluded from the positive prior because burn scars cause sharp drop in NIR reflectance (loss of mesophyll scattering), making NIR negatively correlated with the burn-scar class. EuroSAT. EuroSAT provides 13-band Sentinel-2 imagery spanning the visible, red-edge, NIR, and SWIR spectral regions. We assign class-specific priors based on the physical reflectance properties of each land-cover type: Vegetation classes (AnnualCrop, Forest, HerbaceousVegetation, Pasture, PermanentCrop). We use the red-edge (B05B07, 705783 nm) and NIR (B08/B8A, 842/865 nm) bands as priors. Healthy vegetation produces strong NIR reflectance through mesophyll scattering and exhibits steep rededge transition driven by chlorophyll absorption [Clevers et al., 2002, Delegido et al., 2011]. These bands underpin NDVI, NDRE, and related vegetation indices that have been used operationally for crop monitoring and forest mapping for decades [Tucker, 1979, Rouse et al., 1974]. Industrial. The priors are the SWIR bands (B11, B12; 1610/2190 nm). Impervious surfaces such as concrete, asphalt, and metal roofing reflect strongly in the SWIR due to low moisture content and high mineral reflectance [Zha et al., 2003, Xu, 2008]. Highway, Residential, River, SeaLake. No positive prior is assigned. These classes are spectrally heterogeneous (Highway, Residential) or uniformly low-reflectance (water bodies), so no single band subset has reliably positive association with the class decision. In both datasets, we conservatively include only prior bands with well-documented, physically grounded positive correlation with the target class. Classes without clear positive spectral signature receive an empty prior set and are excluded from the hit-rate evaluation. This design ensures that the spectral validity metric tests whether the attribution method recovers known physical relationships, rather than fitting to arbitrary band rankings.
